drills.q: Name the four C4 levels, the box count for each, and which you draw in a 45-minute round.
drills.a: L1 Context: your system plus users and external systems, 5-8 boxes, no internals, worth 60 seconds only if scope is genuinely contested. L2 Container: separately deployable/runnable things with technology and edge labels, 8-15 boxes, THE interview diagram. L3 Component: modules inside one container, 5-8 boxes, deep dive only and in fresh space. L4 Code: classes, effectively dead, never draw it.

drills.q: Label this edge properly: a browser calling an API gateway on a feed read.
drills.a: HTTPS/JSON, sync, 6 KB, 15k rps peak. Grammar is protocol/format, sync-or-async (both mandatory), payload size, rate or latency. Solid line for sync, dashed for async, consistent within the diagram. Arrow direction means initiates, not data flow, and say which convention you are using because both are common.

drills.q: What is the first thing you do on a blank whiteboard, and why does it matter more than any box?
drills.a: Divide the board: ~20% left for requirements, NFRs, and computed numbers (never erased), ~55% middle for the container diagram, ~25% right kept empty until roughly minute 30 for deep dives. Then place two anchors, client far left and primary datastore far right. This prevents the two classic failures: running out of room on the right, and erasing the requirements you need to point at when justifying a decision at minute 35.

drills.q: State your drawing order and justify why the read path goes first.
drills.a: Anchors, then happy-path read end to end unbroken, then write path below it from the same entry point, then async path below a visible horizontal line, then annotate numbers in a second pass, then deep dives in the right column. Read first because it is usually the latency-critical path and because a complete narrow path is more convincing than a broad incomplete one. The horizontal async line is itself a claim: nothing below it blocks the user. For an ingestion system the order inverts, since the rule generalises to 'draw the path the hard requirement lives on first'.

drills.q: Your diagram has 30 boxes. Fix it in three moves.
drills.a: 1) Delete infrastructure that touches everything and name it in a text line instead: auth, logging/tracing, CI/CD, DNS, per-hop load balancers, mesh sidecars. 2) Collapse replicas into multipliers, so 12 boxes become one box plus 'x12 (3 AZ)'. 3) Group survivors into 3-5 labelled regions (edge, read path, write path, async, storage) so the reader chunks rather than scans. Target 12-15 boxes, since working memory is ~7 plus or minus 2. Then write a 'not drawn:' line so omissions read as scoping decisions.

drills.q: Do the scale-annotation pass on a finished container diagram. Six steps, in order.
drills.a: 1) Rate on the hot edges only (15k rps, 250k inserts/s). 2) Size on stateful boxes (1.6 TB, 100M vectors at 132 GB). 3) Replica count as a multiplier with spread (x12, 3 AZ). 4) Bottleneck double-boxed with the constraint that binds (Redis timelines, 1.6 TB, memory-bound, breaks first at 10x). 5) Partition key on every sharded store. 6) A 'not drawn' line. Second pass only; annotating while drawing means you never finish the path. If you can keep one annotation, keep the bottleneck marker.

drills.q: The interviewer asks where the latency goes in a RAG query. Which diagram, and what must it show?
drills.a: A sequence diagram, because a container diagram cannot express order or time. Show per-hop latency on every arrow: JWT verify 0.2 ms, answer-cache lookup 0.4 ms, query embed 8 ms, ANN top-50 12 ms, cross-encoder rerank 35 ms, LLM first token 420 ms, so TTFT p99 is ~476 ms and the LLM is 88% of it, which means cutting the reranker to 10 ms saves about 5% of perceived time. Also show the async escape as a dashed line to Kafka, the cache-hit path at ~0.6 ms total, and if there is time a failure variant (vector DB times out at 50 ms, breaker opens, fall back to Postgres full-text keyword search with a degraded flag).

drills.q: Draw the ingestion pipeline for a document Q&A service as a dataflow diagram. What five things must appear?
drills.a: Stages left to right: crawler (incremental by mtime, 50k docs/day) to parse (PDF/DOCX/HTML to text, ~30 GB/day, ~0.5% failure) to chunker (512 tokens, 64 overlap, 2.5M chunks/day) to embed (BGE-large 1024-dim, batch 256, ~29 chunks/s, the narrow stage) to idempotent upsert into the vector store plus Postgres metadata. Must appear: volume on every edge; the narrow stage marked with the burst policy (a 500k-doc dump is 25M chunks, about 10 days, so bulk onboarding needs a separate spot-GPU burst path); the DLQ with its failure rate and alert threshold; the idempotency key (doc_id, chunk_index, content_hash) so re-crawl is free; and the freshness SLO with the owning stage (p99 15 min, dominated by the crawler interval).

drills.q: You drew AZ boundaries on a deployment diagram. Prove the multi-AZ claim is real, then say whether losing an AZ is fine.
drills.a: The claim lives in replica placement, not the boundary lines. Stateless: 12 replicas spread by topology constraints across 3 AZs. Stateful is where it fails: a StatefulSet of 4 shards x 2 replicas is 8 pods across 3 AZs, so without pod anti-affinity guaranteeing a shard's two replicas land in different AZs, one AZ loss can take a whole shard. For quorum systems state the arithmetic per AZ, since 3 replicas across 2 AZs cannot survive losing the AZ holding two. Losing an AZ is only fine if provisioned for: 12 replicas sized at 60% utilisation become 8 at 90%, which is past the knee, so p99 roughly triples during the incident. Provision 1.5x so N-1 capacity still sits at target.

drills.q: For a multi-tenant document Q&A system, what is the single highest-value annotation on the dataflow diagram, and why?
drills.a: That the vector-store ACL filter is an optimisation, not the security boundary. A SharePoint permission change flows through an acl.changed event to a sync worker that updates acl_hash on affected chunks with no re-embedding needed, target p99 propagation 60 s. Until it propagates a user could match a stale-allowed chunk, so the FINAL authorisation check happens at read time against Postgres. Marking that distinction is what separates a multi-tenant design from a single-tenant one with a tenant column, and interviewers probe it hard.

drills.q: Two candidates draw identical boxes; one scores, one does not. Explain the difference and why it is not just cosmetic.
drills.a: The scoring diagram has a bracketed technology in every box, protocol plus sync/async on every edge, rates on hot edges, size and partition key on stateful boxes, replica counts as multipliers, a marked bottleneck, and a 'not drawn' line, so the interviewer can point at an edge and ask about p99 and failure behaviour. The other forces them to spend questions on comprehension. It is not cosmetic because labelling is a forcing function: you cannot write 'sync, p99 12 ms' without deciding that hop's latency and consistency properties, or a partition key without deciding the access pattern, so labellers find their own gaps at minute 25 rather than having the interviewer find them at minute 40.

drills.q: When is each of the four diagram types the WRONG choice?
drills.a: C4 context: wrong when scope is obvious (a URL shortener has no interesting external systems), so 90 seconds there is 90 seconds not spent on key generation. Sequence: wrong unprompted in a 45-minute round, since it costs 4-5 minutes to answer a question that may never be asked; narrate it verbally over the container diagram instead. Dataflow: wrong for a request-response service where order matters more than transformation. Deployment: wrong for a logic question about consistency or data modelling, where drawing AZs and instance types is displacement activity. And C4 level 4 is always wrong; if they want that depth, write code.
